Medieval Halloween: Soul Cakes and Bells | History for Sleep

Watch on YouTube Listen on YouTube Music

Medieval Halloween history for sleep: a calm, two-hour night on All Hallows' Eve in a late-medieval English village, with soul cakes, souling, and church bells rung all night for the souls of the dead.

What about the Eve of All Hallows: Medieval Halloween?

The lane through the village is packed earth, with a cobbled stretch near the church where the carts turn. It's dry tonight. The ruts from the harvest wagons have hardened, and a few brown leaves from the elms lie in them like little boats. On either side stand the houses. They're timber framed, with walls of wattle and daub washed in pale ochre and cream, and roofs of thatch that has gone grey and soft with the years. A few of the better houses, near the church, are built of the local stone, honey coloured, with small deep windows.

What about Baking Medieval Soul Cakes?

Let's go back down the lane, to Agnes's house, where the oven is ready. She lit it two hours ago, with a big armful of brushwood and dry furze, and let it roar inside the brick dome until the inside walls glowed white. Then she raked the embers out with a long iron rake and swept the oven floor clean with a damp broom of twigs. Now the oven is full of heat, stored in the brick, and it will bake for an hour or more without any fire inside it at all.

What about Souling: Soul, Soul, for a Soul Cake?

Down in the lane, the morning comes slowly, grey and soft, with a mist lying in the hollows of the fields. The bells have stopped at last. The ringers have gone home to sleep. And it's 1 November, the feast of All Saints. At Agnes's door, the basket of soul cakes is waiting. One candle has burned out in the night. Agnes lights it again. Before long, the first visitor comes. It's an old man called Simon, imagined, who lives alone in a hovel at the end of the village and does odd jobs for anyone who'll have him.

What about All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day?

Let's go back to our village, on the morning of 1 November, around the year 1500. The mist is lifting from the fields. The sun comes up pale and low behind the elms, and the dew on the churchyard grass catches the light like a scattering of tiny glass beads. The rooks are already busy in the stubble. It's the feast of All Saints, one of the great holy days of the year. Nobody works in the fields today. The plough stays in the barn, the loom stands still, and after breakfast, the whole village walks up the lane to the church.

What about Wittenberg, 1517: The Eve of All Saints?

Now let's leave England for a little while, and travel east, across the sea and across the low countries, to a small town on the river Elbe, in Saxony. Its name is Wittenberg. It's 31 October, 1517. The same night as our village vigil, though some years later. All Hallows' Eve. Wittenberg is not a big place. It has a castle, a university only fifteen years old, a market square, and narrow streets of tall timbered houses. And it has a church attached to the castle, the church of All Saints.

What about the Bells Fall Silent?

Back in England, things changed slowly at first, and then all at once. In the 1530s, King Henry the Eighth broke with the Pope in Rome and made himself the head of the church in England. Many of the old customs carried on for a while. But over the next twenty years, one by one, they were questioned, restricted, and taken away. And among them was the ringing of the bells on All Hallows' night. In January 1546, the Archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Cranmer, wrote to the king about several old customs he thought should be stopped.

What about Lights for the Souls?

On the evening of 1 November, if you walk into a cemetery in Poland, you'll see something you'll never forget. The cemetery glows. On every grave, there are candles. Not one or two, but dozens, in little glass jars, red and amber and clear and white, flickering in the dusk. Some graves are covered in them. Paths that would be dark on any other night are lit by thousands of tiny flames. People walk slowly between the rows, talking quietly, stopping to tidy a grave, to add a candle, to light one that's gone out.

About this sleep story

About 1 hour 57 min, narrated slowly for sleep, with no ad breaks. Made as history to fall asleep to: it's fine to drift off partway, and the chapters below let you find your place again.

This episode began with one line in a parish account book from Heybridge in Essex, 1517: eightpence paid to John Gidney of Maldon "for a new bell-rope agenste Hallowmasse". A new rope, bought because the bells would be rung through the night for the souls of the dead. We followed that rope back into the village it served.

0:00:00Intro · 179 words

In 1517, a parish in Essex paid for a new bell rope before Hallowmass, when English church bells were rung for the souls of the dead.

This is Dreaming Ages. Over the next two hours, we'll bake soul cakes on All Hallows' Eve, hear the bells rung all night, and follow a medieval Halloween across Europe. Nothing loud, nothing sudden, and nothing frightening. Just a slow voice, a warm oven, and the sound of faraway bells.

Pull up the blanket, rest your head on the pillow, and I'll blow out the candle. Now, follow me back in time.

Intro

It's the last evening of October, around the year 1500, in a small English village. The light is going amber over the stubble fields. Rooks are drifting home to the tall elms by the church, calling to each other in their rough, comfortable voices. In the lane, someone is carrying a pail of milk, walking slowly so as not to spill it.

The customs are real. The village and its people are imagined, and when we're picturing something, we'll say so.

0:01:26The Eve of All Hallows: Medieval Halloween · 850 words

The lane through the village is packed earth, with a cobbled stretch near the church where the carts turn. It's dry tonight. The ruts from the harvest wagons have hardened, and a few brown leaves from the elms lie in them like little boats.

On either side stand the houses. They're timber framed, with walls of wattle and daub washed in pale ochre and cream, and roofs of thatch that has gone grey and soft with the years. A few of the better houses, near the church, are built of the local stone, honey coloured, with small deep windows. Smoke rises from every roof, not from chimneys, mostly, but seeping up through the thatch itself, from the hearths in the middle of the floors.

The harvest is in. It has been in for weeks. The barns are full of sheaves waiting for the flail, and the apples have been picked and laid out in rows on the slatted floors of the lofts, not touching, so that one bad apple won't spoil its neighbours. The wheat for next year is already in the ground. There's an old farming rhyme by Thomas Tusser, printed later in the 1500s, that tells you to leave off sowing wheat before Hallowmas Eve. The men of this village would agree. The ploughs have been scraped and hung up in the barns. The oxen are standing in their stalls, warm and patient, breathing out clouds of sweet hay.

And so the year has turned. The busy months are over. The long evenings of autumn have arrived.

Let's walk up the lane, toward the church.

Halfway up, on the left, there's a low house with a wide door and a little lean-to at the back, built against a hump of brick and clay. That's an oven. It belongs to Agnes. She's imagined, but she's the kind of woman every English village had: a widow who earns a little by baking for her neighbours. People bring her their dough on baking days, and she bakes it for a farthing or a handful of flour. Tonight, though, she's baking for no one in particular. She's baking for everyone.

The door is open, and the warm smell of bread drifts out into the lane.

Inside, the fire on the hearth has burned down to a deep red glow. On the big table, scrubbed pale with sand, there are rows of small round cakes, each about the size of the palm of a hand, set out on a cloth to rise. Agnes is moving slowly along the rows, pressing a cross into the top of each one with the back of a knife. She doesn't hurry. She's done this every year since she was a girl, at her own mother's side.

These are soul cakes. Tomorrow, and the day after, she'll give them away. To the poor who come to the door, to the children, to anyone who asks. And each person who takes one is asked to say a prayer for the souls of the dead. For her husband, who died three years ago. For her mother and father. For all Christian souls.

In the corner, by the fire, her grandson Wat is sitting on a stool, eating the end of a heel of bread. He's twelve, and tonight is a special night for him. For the first time, the ringers have said he can come up the church tower with them, and help.

He keeps glancing at the door.

"Not yet," says Agnes, without looking up. "They won't start till the light's gone. Eat your bread."

Let's leave them for a moment and walk on.

At the top of the lane, the land rises a little, and there stands the church. It's the biggest building anyone in the village has ever been inside. Its walls are grey stone, and its tower is square and solid, with narrow openings near the top where the bells hang. The tower was built by the grandfathers of the oldest people in the village, and paid for, a little at a time, by everyone.

Around the church lies the churchyard, green and quiet, with a low wall around it and a wooden gate with a little roof over it, the lychgate. There are almost no gravestones here. Only the richest families have stones. Everyone else lies beneath the grass, with perhaps a wooden cross that has long since rotted away. But the village knows where they are. The old people can walk you round the churchyard and tell you who lies under every hummock of turf.

In the church porch, a man in a long dark gown is standing with a ring of iron keys. That's Hugh, the parish clerk, also imagined. He helps the priest, leads the responses, keeps the church clean, and tonight he'll help organise the ringing. He's looking up at the tower, where the last of the light is catching the stone.

The sky has turned from amber to rose, and from rose to a soft dove grey. The first star appears above the tower.

It's the eve of All Hallows.

0:08:00Three Holy Days · 766 words

In these years, nobody in the village calls this night Halloween. They call it All Hallows' Eve, or All Hallows' even, the evening before the feast of All Hallows. Hallow is an old English word for a holy person, a saint. And tomorrow, 1 November, is the feast of All Saints. The day after that, 2 November, is All Souls.

So this isn't one night. It's the doorway into three days, which people call Hallowtide. And each of the three has its own meaning.

All Hallows' Eve, tonight, is a vigil, a night of waiting and watching before a great feast. All Saints, tomorrow, celebrates all the holy men and women in heaven, the famous ones with their own feast days and the countless unknown ones without. And All Souls, the day after, is for everyone else. For all the ordinary dead. For the people under the grass in the churchyard. For Agnes's husband, and her mother and father, and for all the people the village has ever lost.

How did these days come to sit together, here at the end of October?

The story goes back a long way, to Rome. Early Christians remembered the martyrs, the people who had died for their faith, on the anniversaries of their deaths. But as the centuries passed, there were more saints than there were days in the year. And so the idea grew of one feast for all of them together.

In Rome, in the year six hundred and nine or six hundred and ten, Pope Boniface the Fourth took over an old temple, the Pantheon, with its great round dome, and dedicated it to Mary and all the martyrs, on 13 May. For a long time, that was the day.

Then, in the seven hundred and thirties, Pope Gregory the Third consecrated a chapel in the old basilica of Saint Peter to all the saints, and, by many accounts, fixed its anniversary on 1 November. About a century later, Pope Gregory the Fourth extended the November feast to the whole Western church. In the year eight hundred and thirty five, at the Pope's request, the emperor Louis the Pious, the son of Charlemagne, ordered it kept throughout his lands.

Why November? Nobody wrote down a reason that everyone agrees on. Historians still discuss it. Some point to the Celtic new year, which also fell at the start of November. Others think the date simply came from that chapel in Rome. We'll leave that question where it is, and let it rest.

What we do know is that, by our night, around the year 1500, 1 November had been All Saints for more than six hundred years.

All Souls came a little later.

In the late nine hundreds and early 1000s, there was a great monastery at Cluny, in Burgundy, in what is now eastern France. Its abbot was a man called Odilo. He was remembered for his charity, and for feeding the poor in years of hunger. He ordered that, in all the monasteries that looked to Cluny, the day after All Saints should be kept for all the faithful departed. On that day, the monks would pray and say masses not for the saints, who didn't need them, but for all the dead.

Tradition says Odilo made this rule in the year nine hundred and ninety eight. One modern study argues that it was a little later, perhaps around 1030. Either way, the custom spread from Cluny to other monasteries, and from the monasteries to the cathedrals, and from the cathedrals to the parish churches. It spread through France, and Germany, and England. And in the 1200s, even Rome took it up. By our night, 2 November had been All Souls' Day for centuries.

And so the three days came together. Tonight, the vigil. Tomorrow, the saints in heaven. The day after, all the souls of the dead.

For the people of our village, the third day matters most. They don't know many saints personally. But they all know someone who has died.

Back in the lane, the light is nearly gone. A cart rumbles past, its driver walking at the ox's head. A woman calls her children in. In the doorways, here and there, small lights appear. Rushlights, mostly, made from the pith of rushes dipped in fat, and a few candles of tallow, which smell of the kitchen. In the church, there are candles of beeswax, which smell sweet and clean, and which are far too expensive for anyone to burn at home.

Hugh is going into the church now, to light them.

0:13:47Why the Dead Needed Prayers · 835 words

To understand why Agnes is baking, and why the ringers will climb the tower tonight, we need to step inside the minds of the people in this village, and look at how they pictured the world after death.

They believed, as their church taught, that when a person dies, their soul goes on. A very few, the saints, go straight to heaven. But most people, even good people, aren't quite ready for heaven when they die. They've done small wrongs they never made up for. They've been unkind, or proud, or careless, and never quite put it right. And so, the church taught, most souls pass first through a place of cleansing, a place of waiting and putting right. It was called purgatory.

People pictured it in many ways. Preachers often described it in hard terms, to make their listeners think about how they lived. But at the heart of the idea was something hopeful. Every soul in purgatory was on its way to heaven. It was a waiting room, not a prison. And the wait could be shortened.

That's the key to everything that happens tonight. The living could help the dead.

They could help by praying. By having masses said. By giving alms to the poor, in the name of the dead person, so that the poor would pray for them in turn. Every prayer, every candle, every loaf given away was thought of as a kindness sent across the gap between the living and the dead.

And so, in every parish in England, the dead were remembered, by name, again and again.

When someone died, there was the funeral, with candles around the coffin and the bell tolling. A month later, there was the month's mind, a mass to remember them a month on. A year later, the year's mind. Families who could afford it paid for masses to be said for years afterwards. The richest built chantries, little chapels or altars with a priest paid to pray for their souls forever. Some left money in their wills for candles to burn before a favourite statue, or for bread to be given to the poor on the anniversary of their death.

Those with very little money joined together. Many villages had a guild, a sort of club of neighbours, who paid a few pence a year. In return, when a member died, the guild would pay for their funeral candles, gather to pray for them, and remember them every year.

And in many churches there was a long list called the bede roll. The word bede is an old word for a prayer. The bede roll held the names of all the people of the parish who had given something to the church, a cloth for the altar, a few shillings toward the new tower, a sheep, a candle. On certain Sundays, the priest would read the names aloud, and ask the people to pray for them. The names of men and women dead for a hundred years would be spoken again in the church they had helped to build.

It's easy to imagine what that felt like, sitting on the floor or standing in the nave, hearing the name of your own grandmother read out, among all the others. The village went on, together, the living and the dead.

All Souls' Day was the great day for all of this. On that one day, the whole church prayed for all the dead together. Not just the ones with money for masses. Not just the ones in the guild. Everyone. All Christian souls.

And there were two things, above all, that people did on the night before.

They gave bread.

And they rang the bells.

A book of sermons printed in the early 1500s, called the Festyvall, puts the first of these very simply. In its old spelling, it says that in old times, good people would bake bread on All Hallows' Day and give it out for all Christian souls. That's what Agnes is doing tonight. That's what the soul cakes are for. Every cake given away is a little prayer sent out into the dark.

As for the bells, people believed, as their grandparents had, that the sound of a church bell carried prayer with it. A bell rung for the dead called the living to pray. And some said that the sound itself was a comfort to the souls in waiting, a reminder that they had not been forgotten.

So tonight, while the village sleeps, or tries to, the bells will go on. Not loud and wild, but steady. A long, slow, patient sound, rolling out over the fields and the orchards and the sleeping houses, all through the night.

Up at the church, Hugh has lit the candles. Through the open door, you can see them burning on the altar, small and golden in the great grey dark of the nave.

Down the lane, in Agnes's house, the first tray of soul cakes is ready for the oven.

0:19:54Baking Medieval Soul Cakes · 1,031 words

Let's go back down the lane, to Agnes's house, where the oven is ready.

She lit it two hours ago, with a big armful of brushwood and dry furze, and let it roar inside the brick dome until the inside walls glowed white. Then she raked the embers out with a long iron rake and swept the oven floor clean with a damp broom of twigs. Now the oven is full of heat, stored in the brick, and it will bake for an hour or more without any fire inside it at all.

Wat comes to stand beside her. He knows this part. He's watched it every year.

Agnes slides a long flat wooden paddle, a peel, under the first row of soul cakes, and with a quick small push of her wrists, she sets them down on the hot floor of the oven. Another row. And another. Then she closes the oven mouth with an iron door, and seals the edges with a smear of wet clay, so no heat escapes.

Now there's nothing to do but wait. Agnes sits down on the bench by the fire, and folds her hands, and closes her eyes for a moment.

What exactly is in a soul cake?

The honest answer is that it depended on where you lived, and on how much you had. The oldest descriptions are simple. People baked bread. Not a special recipe, just good bread, made from whatever grain the household had. A writer in the 1600s, describing the customs of the old faith, mentions soul mass cakes in Lancashire and Herefordshire that were a kind of oat cake, which the better off families gave to the poor on All Souls' Day. And the poor, in return, would say a short old couplet. In the old country speech, it went: God have your saul, beens and all. Which most likely means, God have your soul, bones and all.

Later, in the 1800s, when folklorists began collecting old customs, soul cakes had become something richer. A Shropshire family kept the recipe their grandmother had used: flour and a little butter, sugar, yeast, eggs, a good pinch of allspice, and enough new milk to make a light dough, shaped into flattish round buns. Sweet, and spiced, and soft. A treat.

Agnes's cakes are somewhere in between. They're imagined, so we can choose. Let's say she's used wheat flour, which is a little extravagant, and a spoonful of honey, and a handful of currants she bought at the market town at Michaelmas. And the cross on top, pressed in with the back of a knife, so that everyone will know what these cakes are for.

While they bake, the smell fills the house. Warm bread and honey and the faint dark sweetness of the currants. It drifts out through the open door, into the lane, where the night is cool and still. Somewhere down the lane, a dog lifts its head and sniffs the air, and then settles down again with its nose on its paws.

Agnes isn't the only one baking tonight. All along the lane, in kitchens and at hearths, other women are doing the same, each in her own way. Some have made flat oat cakes on an iron griddle over the fire. Some have made little loaves. A farmer's wife at the big house by the church has made a whole basket full, enough for every poor family in the parish. Tomorrow, and the day after, the poor of the village will go from door to door, and at every door, they'll be given something, and they'll promise to pray.

This wasn't begging, the way we might think of it. It was more like an exchange. The household gave bread. The poor gave prayers. Both sides helped the dead. And the poor, who had so little, had something real to offer, something the rich needed. In a world where almost everything depended on how much land and money you had, this was one of the few nights of the year when that balance tipped, just a little, the other way.

After about half an hour, Agnes stands, and goes to the oven, and taps the clay seal with the edge of the peel, and it cracks and falls away. She opens the door. A breath of heat rolls out into the room, and the smell of the bread is suddenly much stronger.

The soul cakes have risen and turned golden brown. The crosses on top have opened a little in the oven, so that each one shows a pale line against the darker crust.

One by one, Agnes lifts them out with the peel, and turns them onto a cloth on the table to cool. Wat counts them under his breath. Thirty six. Agnes lets him take one, still warm, and he breaks it open, and the steam rises from the soft white middle, and he eats it slowly, by the fire.

"Remember," says Agnes, "that one's for your grandfather."

Wat nods, with his mouth full, and thinks of his grandfather, whom he can only just remember. A big man, with a beard, who used to carry him on his shoulders to the harvest field. And for a moment, in the warm kitchen, with the taste of honey and currants on his tongue, it's almost as if the old man is there.

When the cakes have cooled a little, Agnes lays them in a wide, shallow basket of woven willow, lined with a clean cloth. She sets the basket on the bench just inside the door, where anyone passing can see it. And she lights two candles, and puts one on either side.

It's the scene from the very start of our journey. The basket of soul cakes, round and golden, each marked with its little cross. The two candles, burning steadily in the still air. And beyond the door, the dark lane, leading up the hill to the church.

Up at the top of the lane, a light appears in the narrow openings of the church tower. The ringers have gone up.

Wat jumps to his feet.

"Go on, then," says Agnes. "And mind the steps."

0:27:09The Bells All Night · 829 words

Before we follow Wat up the hill, let's look at how we know about this night at all. Because the bells of All Hallows left a trail behind them, in a place you might not expect. Not in poems or chronicles, but in accounts.

Every English parish had churchwardens, usually two of them, chosen each year from among the villagers. They looked after the church building and everything in it, and the money that paid for it all. And every year, they wrote down what they'd spent. A few pence for candles. A few shillings for mending the roof. A penny for a new lock on the church chest. Many of these account books survive, kept in county archives, in faded brown ink on thick paper and parchment. And in them, year after year, as the end of October drew near, the same kinds of entries appear. Payments for the bells.

In 1517, the churchwardens of Heybridge, a small parish in Essex near the town of Maldon, set down their spending for the season. They paid for frankincense, against Hallowmass. They paid a man from Maldon for mending the clapper of the third bell, against Hallowmass. And they paid another man of Maldon for a new bell rope, against Hallowmass. That word, against, in the old sense, means in time for, or ready for. Everything had to be in order before the great night came.

At Leverton, in Lincolnshire, in 1524, the wardens paid a carpenter named William Josson for helping with the belfry against Hallowmass. Two years later, they paid a wright named Rodley for mending the bells against the same feast. Five pence the first time, four pence the second. Small sums, carefully counted.

And at Bishop's Stortford, in Hertfordshire, they paid for making a new bell wheel, against All Hallowtide. That's the big wooden wheel fixed to the side of a bell, which the rope runs around, so that a ringer can swing the bell high.

Why so much care, so much mending, so close to the end of October? Because on the night before All Saints, and in many places on the night of All Saints too, going into All Souls, the bells would be rung for hours. In some places, all night long. A bell with a loose clapper, or a rope that was wearing thin, would never last the night.

And this ringing wasn't free. Ropes cost money. Ringers grew thirsty. Somebody had to pay. In the great church of Holy Trinity in Coventry, in 1462, the rules for the church's officers set down exactly how it should be done. On All Hallows' Day at evening, the first deacon was to go among the people on the north side of the church and gather money from them, for the ringers that ring for Christian souls. And the second deacon was to do the same on the south side.

It's a small, practical sentence. But think what it means. On that evening, all those years ago, the people of Coventry, standing in their great church, reached into their purses and gave a coin, so that the bells would ring through the night for the dead. Every coin dropped into the deacon's hand was a share in the ringing. A share in the remembering.

0:41:50The Voice of the Bell · 932 words

While the ringers rest at midnight, let's look up, past the ceiling of the ringing chamber, to the bells themselves.

If Wat climbed the ladder through the trapdoor, he'd find himself in the bell chamber, near the top of the tower. It's a cold, airy room, open to the night through tall slatted windows, so that the sound can pour out over the fields. And there, hanging in a great frame of oak beams, are the bells. Three of them, in our imagined village. Dark bronze, dull green in places, each one bigger than a barrel, each one hanging mouth down, very still now, with the lantern light just catching the curve of its shoulder.

A medieval bell was made of bell metal, a kind of bronze. Roughly speaking, about four parts copper to one part tin. Copper alone would be too soft, and give a dull note. Too much tin, and the bell would be brittle, and might crack. Bellfounders learned the right mixture over generations, and guarded their skill.

Casting a bell was hard, heavy, dangerous work. A big bell was difficult to move along muddy medieval roads, so very often, the bellfounder came to the church instead. He and his men would dig a pit, sometimes in the churchyard itself, or in a field nearby, and build the mould right there.

The mould was made of loam. That's soft moulding clay, bound together with calves' hair and bands of hay, so that it would hold its shape and not crack as it dried. First, they built up the inside shape of the bell, called the core, on a framework of bricks. Then, over that, they shaped a false bell, exactly the shape the real bell would be. And over that, a thick outer case. When everything had dried and baked hard, they lifted off the case, broke away the false bell, and put the case back over the core, leaving a narrow empty space between them, exactly the shape of the bell.

Then came the great day. A furnace was lit, and the copper and tin were melted, until the metal ran bright and liquid. And the molten bronze was poured into the mould, glowing orange in the dusk, and hissing, and smoking. Then everyone waited, for days, and for a big bell even weeks, while the metal cooled slowly in the earth.

Picture the people of a village, gathered at the edge of the pit, watching. When a bell was cast in the church or the churchyard, there was great excitement, and people brought pots and pans and other household things of metal to add to the casting. At Bridgwater, in Somerset, as long ago as 1284, the records show the townspeople giving their metal for a new bell. A little of their own households would be in the bell, and its voice would carry a little of them.

When the bell was cold, they dug it out of the earth, cleaned it, and struck it, and heard its voice for the first time. If the note wasn't quite right, the founder could put it right a little with a file or a whetstone, as an old monk's instructions for bell making advised.

And before a new bell was hung in the tower, it was often blessed. People called this, informally, the baptism of the bell. The bell was washed with holy water, anointed, and given a name. Very often, the name of a saint. A bell might be called Mary, or Gabriel, or Katherine, or John. And the name was sometimes cast into the bronze itself, around the shoulder of the bell, in a line of raised letters, often with a short prayer in Latin. Holy Mary, pray for us. Saint John, pray for us. Many old English bells still carry inscriptions like these.

So a medieval bell wasn't just a thing. In a way, it was a voice. People spoke of bells almost as if they were alive. Bells called people to church. They told the hours. They warned of fire, and of danger. And, people believed, they could do more than that.

There's an old Latin verse, found on some bells in Europe, that sums up what a bell was thought to do. Part of it says, I mourn the dead, I break the lightning, I call to the sabbath. Many people believed that the sound of a blessed bell could drive away storms, and keep evil spirits at a distance. It's one reason bells were sometimes rung during thunderstorms.

And above all, the bell spoke for the dead. When someone in the parish was dying, a bell was rung, called the passing bell, so that everyone who heard it would stop for a moment and pray for the soul that was passing. Then, after a death, the bell would toll, slowly. And in later centuries, in many places, the number of strokes at the end of the tolling told the village whether a man, a woman, or a child had died, so that people in the fields would know, and could guess who it was.

That's why, on All Hallows' night, it felt right to ring. The bells were the voice of the parish. And on this one night, that voice was raised for all the dead at once.

Up in the bell chamber, a little wind moves through the slatted windows. One of the bells hums, very faintly, the way bells do, even when nobody rings them. And then, down below, the ringers stand, and stretch, and take hold of the ropes again.

A soul cake, a soul cake, have mercy on all Christian souls, for a soul cake.

On the evening of All Souls, or All Saints, small bands of children went from house to house, knocking at the doors of the farms and the bigger houses, and singing. The songs varied from village to village, and the people who collected them wrote down dozens of versions. But many shared the same verses.

Soul, soul, for a soul cake. I pray you, good mistress, a soul cake. An apple or pear, a plum or a cherry, any good thing to make us merry. One for Peter, two for Paul, three for Him who made us all.

You can almost hear it. The children standing in the lane in the dusk, their breath misting, singing in a slow chant on two notes, over and over, until the door opened.

Now let's leave England for a little while, and travel east, across the sea and across the low countries, to a small town on the river Elbe, in Saxony. Its name is Wittenberg.

It's 31 October, 1517. The same night as our village vigil, though some years later. All Hallows' Eve.

Wittenberg is not a big place. It has a castle, a university only fifteen years old, a market square, and narrow streets of tall timbered houses. And it has a church attached to the castle, the church of All Saints. On the eve of All Saints, this church was getting ready for its great feast.

The ruler of Saxony, the Elector Frederick, had gathered in this church a huge collection of holy relics. Bones of saints, scraps of cloth, splinters of wood, each in its own little case of silver or crystal or gold. On the feast of All Saints, the relics were put on display, and people came from far around to see them. And by honouring the relics, the church taught, they could receive an indulgence. A shortening, it was promised, of the time a soul would spend in purgatory.

You can see the connection to our village. The same idea, the same hope. That the living could do something, could give something, to shorten the waiting of souls.

Let's picture that evening in Wittenberg. We're imagining the details, but the shape of it is real. The autumn dark comes early over the flat land by the river. In the castle church, the sacristans are busy, unlocking cupboards, lifting out the reliquaries one by one, wiping them with soft cloths, setting them out in their places. The candlelight catches the silver and the crystal, so that the whole church seems to glitter. Outside, in the lanes, there are more people than usual, visitors from the villages around, finding beds in inns and in the houses of relatives, ready for the feast tomorrow. Somewhere a cart rattles over the cobbles. Somewhere a dog barks. And the bells of the town, like the bells of a thousand other towns that night, are ringing.

But in Wittenberg, there was a monk, and a teacher at the university, who had begun to have doubts. His name was Martin Luther.

Luther was troubled by the way indulgences were being preached and sold. A preacher named Johann Tetzel was travelling through the towns near Wittenberg, raising money for the building of the great new basilica of Saint Peter in Rome, and people were going to hear him and buy indulgences, for themselves and for their dead. To Luther, it seemed that something meant to be about true sorrow and true change of heart had become a matter of payment.

So on 31 October, 1517, the eve of All Saints, Luther wrote a letter to the archbishop responsible for the preaching, Albrecht of Mainz. And with it, he sent a list of ninety five points, or theses, in Latin, that he wanted to debate. Arguments about indulgences, about purgatory, and about what the church could and could not do for souls.

There's a famous picture of what happened next. Luther, with a hammer, nailing his theses to the door of the castle church. It's one of the best known scenes in European history. But historians aren't sure it happened that way. The earliest account of the nailing was written years later, after Luther's death. Some historians think he did post the theses on the church door, which was a common place for notices at the university. Others think he only sent them by letter. It remains a question, and we'll leave it as one.

Either way, he chose his day. The eve of All Saints. The night when the relics were about to be shown and the indulgences offered. The night when, all across Europe, bells were ringing for the souls in purgatory.

What happened next took many years, and changed everything. Luther's ideas spread, carried by the new printing presses, much faster than anyone expected. In the years that followed, the churches of Europe divided. And one of the things that divided them was this very question. Can the living help the dead? Do prayers and bread and bells really reach them?

For the people of Wittenberg, on that October night in 1517, it was probably just an ordinary eve of All Saints. The relics were polished. The candles were ready. Somewhere a bell was ringing. In a room near the university, a monk sealed a letter. And very few people, if any, knew that anything had changed.

1:19:53The Bells Fall Silent · 1,043 words

Back in England, things changed slowly at first, and then all at once.

In the 1530s, King Henry the Eighth broke with the Pope in Rome and made himself the head of the church in England. Many of the old customs carried on for a while. But over the next twenty years, one by one, they were questioned, restricted, and taken away. And among them was the ringing of the bells on All Hallows' night.

In January 1546, the Archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Cranmer, wrote to the king about several old customs he thought should be stopped. Among them, as the state papers summarise his letter, was the ringing on All Hallow day at night.

The king agreed. In a letter back to Cranmer, he wrote that because that vigil was abused, like other vigils, it should be abolished. And there should be no watching, nor ringing, except as was commonly done on other holy days at night.

Just like that, the long night of bells was meant to end.

Then, in 1547, Henry died, and his young son Edward became king. Edward's government went further. The chantries, those little chapels and altars where priests had prayed for the souls of the dead, were closed, and their lands and money taken by the crown. The bede rolls stopped being read. The candles for the dead were put out. The whole great structure of prayer for souls, which had stood for centuries, was taken down.

Imagine, for a moment, what this might have felt like in a village like ours. Let's say that Wat is a grown man now, nearly sixty, a thatcher like old Roger, with grandchildren of his own. We're imagining, of course. On the evening of 31 October, he walks up to the church as he always has, out of long habit. And the tower is silent. The ropes hang still. The door is locked.

He stands in the churchyard for a while, in the dusk, listening to the quiet. And then he walks home.

But the story didn't end there. In 1553, Edward died, and his half sister Mary became queen. Mary was a Catholic, and she brought back the old faith, and many of the old customs with it. And the bells came back too.

We know this, again, from the churchwardens' accounts. At Leverton in Lincolnshire, in 1556, the wardens paid nineteen pence and a halfpenny to the ringers on All Hallow night. The bells were rung for the souls once more.

Let's imagine Wat again. He's an old man now, slow on the stairs. But that autumn, the year the bells come back, he climbs the tower one more time. He doesn't ring. His arms aren't strong enough. He sits on the bench in the corner, where he sat as a boy, with his back against the cool stone, and listens to the young men ringing. And he thinks of his grandmother, and his grandfather, and his wife, and old Roger, and everyone.

It didn't last. Mary died in 1558, and her half sister Elizabeth became queen. Elizabeth's church kept a middle way in many things, but on prayers for the dead, it was clear. In 1562, when the leading clergy met in a great assembly called Convocation, one of the proposals put before them asked that the superfluous ringing of bells, and the superstitious ringing of bells at All Hallowtide and on All Souls' Day, with the two nights before and after, be prohibited.

Let's imagine our village once more, in those years. Wat is gone now, buried near his grandmother at the east end of the churchyard. His granddaughter, a young woman named Joan, still lives in the cottage by the church. She bakes, as her family always has. And every autumn, at the end of October, without quite knowing why, she makes a batch of small round cakes, with a little spice, and marks each one with a cross before it goes into the oven. Her mother did it. Her grandmother did it. It's what you do at Hallowtide.

When the village children come to the door on All Saints' morning, singing their song, she gives them a cake each. She doesn't pray for the souls any more, not in the old way. The church has told her that's not needed, and perhaps she believes it. But she still thinks of her family as she hands the cakes out. Her grandfather, and his grandmother before him. The cakes are a way of remembering, even if nobody says so.

On All Hallows' night, in Joan's time, the village is quieter than it used to be. There's no crowd at the church, no candles burning in the nave all night, no ringers climbing the stair with their bread and their jug of ale. The tower stands dark against the stars. But in the cottages, the fires are lit, and families sit around them, and tell stories. Some of the old people remember the bells. They describe them to the children, the way you might describe a place you visited long ago. How the sound carried over the fields. How you could hear it from your bed, all night long, rising and falling with the wind. How it made you feel that the whole parish was awake together, keeping watch.

The children listen, and try to imagine it. And then, one by one, they fall asleep.

And so, slowly, the long night of bells faded from English villages. Not everywhere at once, and not completely. Old habits are strong, and some parishes were slow to change. But within a generation or two, the ringing for the souls on All Hallows' night had mostly gone.

The bells themselves stayed. They still rang for services, for weddings, for great news, and for funerals. In time, English ringers would develop their famous art of change ringing, long patterns of bells rung in ever changing orders, which is still practised today. But the slow, steady ringing all night for the dead became a memory.

And yet, as we'll see, not everything went. Some things are harder to stop than bells. Some things live in kitchens, and in children's songs, and in the habits of families, long after the laws have changed.

1:27:39What Stayed · 1,436 words

The laws changed. The chantries closed. The bells, on All Hallows' night, mostly fell quiet. But the soul cakes stayed.

They stayed for a very long time. For more than three hundred years after Henry the Eighth's letter, in the farmhouses and villages of the north and west of England, people went on baking cakes for the souls at the beginning of November, and children went on knocking at doors and singing for them. Most of them, by then, had no idea where the custom came from. They just knew it was what you did.

We can follow the soul cakes through those centuries in the notes of clergymen and antiquarians, and later of folklorists, people who went about the countryside writing down old customs before they disappeared.

Let's start with a story about money, and bells. In Solihull, which is now part of the city of Birmingham but was then a small market town in Warwickshire, a man named John Collet left money in 1565 for a gift to the poor. That was only a few years after Queen Elizabeth's injunctions. And his gift was still being given out more than two and a half centuries later, in 1826, on All Souls' Day. And how did the poor of Solihull know when to come and collect it? The church bells were rung.

Think about that for a moment. Long after the ringing for the souls had been forbidden, a bell was still ringing on All Souls' Day in that town, calling people to receive a gift given in memory of the dead. The meaning had shifted. But something of the old shape was still there.

In Staffordshire, the cakes were called soul mass cakes, or somas cakes. Somas, said quickly, the way country people said it. In some counties, one old writer noted, the soul mass cake was made on All Souls' Day, 2 November, and always in a triangular shape.

In East Yorkshire, people gave out saumas loaves. And there was a custom there that whoever received one should keep a single cake in the house for the whole year that followed, for good luck. Not to eat. Just to keep, on a shelf, or in a cupboard, until the next autumn came around.

Some people kept them a great deal longer than a year. A history of Whitby, on the Yorkshire coast, written in the early 1800s, mentions a lady there who had one that was more than a hundred years old.

A hundred years. We can imagine it, wrapped in a cloth, dry and hard as wood, kept in a drawer or a tin, handed down from mother to daughter. Baked, perhaps, in the 1760s, by a grandmother she never knew. Never eaten. Just kept, as a small piece of luck, and perhaps as a small piece of memory too.

Up in the Cleveland hills, in the north of Yorkshire, a vicar named John Atkinson wrote a book about the local dialect in 1868. In it, he described soul mass loaves as sets of small square cakes, each worth a farthing, with currants in the centre, which bakers commonly gave to their customers at this time of year. A little gift from the baker. Like a calendar or a box of biscuits that a shop might give a loyal customer at Christmas today.

In Lancashire and in the north east, soul cakes were sometimes called harcakes, a kind of thin parkin, which is a sticky ginger cake made with oatmeal and treacle. In Lancashire and Herefordshire, oat cakes were sometimes given. And in Warwickshire and elsewhere, a Victorian writer noted, seed cake went with Halloween, as a sign of the end of the wheat seed time. Thomas Tusser, back in the 1500s, had a rhyme about that too, the farmer reminding his wife that when the wheat sowing was done, she mustn't forget the seed cake. The last of the sowing done, the fields put to bed until spring, and a cake to mark it.

And in Shropshire, John Aubrey's high heap of soul cakes, set on the table for visitors back in the 1600s, still had its echoes two centuries later. In the 1880s, the folklorist Charlotte Burne was still collecting souling songs and soul cake recipes from Shropshire families. Imagine a farmhouse kitchen, the fire bright in the range, and on the scrubbed table, a pile of little cakes, waiting for whoever might call.

And people did call. Children above all. All through the 1800s, in Cheshire, in Shropshire, in Staffordshire, in parts of Yorkshire and Lancashire, children went souling. They went in little groups, from house to house, in the dark of the evening, or on All Saints' morning. In some places, they carried lanterns made from hollowed out turnips, with a candle inside. And they sang.

The songs changed from place to place. In Oswestry, in Shropshire, right on the border with Wales, the souling songs had Welsh words mixed in. Sometimes grown up soulers went out too, and one of them might bring a concertina to play. And in 1899, a version of the souling song was heard sung by boys in Harrogate, in Yorkshire, as they ran beside a carriage, begging.

Let's imagine one of those evenings, in a Shropshire village, around 1880. We're imagining the people, but not the custom. It's the last day of October, and it's getting dark early. Three children, a girl of ten and her two younger brothers, set out from their cottage with a turnip lantern, its candle glowing through the thin carved walls, so that the face cut into it seems to smile in the dusk.

They walk down the lane, past the smithy, where the fire is banked for the night, and up the track to the big farmhouse on the hill. The yard dog barks, then recognises them, and wags its tail. The girl knocks. And when the door opens, letting out a wedge of warm yellow light and the smell of baking, the three of them sing, all together, a little out of tune.

The farmer's wife listens with her arms folded and a smile on her face. When they've finished, she takes them into the kitchen, where on the table there's a heap of soul cakes, just as the old writers described. They each take one, and she drops an apple into each of their pockets, and a penny into the girl's hand. And then they're off again, down the hill, the lantern swinging, to the next house, singing as they go.

By then, as one writer noted, the memory of begging for bread for the sake of souls departed had faded, leaving only the name, soul cake. The children didn't know they were singing for the dead. They were singing for cakes, and apples, and pennies.

Then, in 1870, came a new law about education. Over the following years, children, other than the very youngest, were expected to be in school. And since souling had mostly been done by children, during the day, the custom began to fade. Teachers didn't want their pupils wandering the lanes on 1 November, singing for cakes.

But it didn't vanish. In rural Cheshire, northern Shropshire, and the nearby parts of Staffordshire, souling carried on into the 1950s. And in 1975, the folklorist Christina Hole wrote that in Cheshire and Shropshire, small bands of children still went souling through the villages, on All Souls' Day or on All Saints' Day, singing one or other of the traditional songs, and receiving gifts of money, or cakes, or sweets.

On the edges of Sheffield, there was a version called caking night. It was held at the end of October or the beginning of November, and children went round saying an old rhyme. Cake, cake, copper, copper. A copper was a penny. And in 1982, it was recorded that they received about ten pence from each householder. Before the Second World War, in the village of Dungworth near Sheffield, children went caking in masks, and asked the people in each house to guess who they were.

And in Cheshire, the soul cakers of Antrobus still perform their play each autumn, with King George, and the Black Prince, and the quack doctor, and the old horse.

So when you hear that the old soul cakes are gone, remember that they went very slowly. Over five hundred years, from the cottage of a widow like Agnes, through the Reformation and the bells falling silent, through the farmhouses and the dialect books and the high heaps on Shropshire tables, all the way into living memory.

1:37:54A Soul Cake by the Fire · 542 words

Before we leave England, let's spend a few quiet minutes in a kitchen, and think about how a soul cake was actually made.

We should say first that we don't have a recipe from Agnes's time. Nobody in a medieval village wrote down how to make soul cakes. You learned it by watching your mother, and she learned by watching hers. The recipes we do have were written down much later, in the seventeen and 1800s and after, and they vary from county to county. But they give us a good idea of the kind of thing a soul cake was.

It was small, and round, and flat, more like a soft biscuit, or a little scone, than a cake in the modern sense. It was usually made with flour, and butter, and a little sugar, and often an egg, and a little milk to bring the dough together. And it was flavoured with spice. Nutmeg, perhaps, or cinnamon, or allspice, or ginger, whatever the household could afford. Many recipes add currants or raisins. Some add a pinch of saffron, which turns the dough a soft golden yellow.

So let's imagine making them, slowly, the way you might on an autumn evening.

You start with the flour, sifted into a big earthenware bowl. Then the butter, cut into small pieces, rubbed into the flour with your fingertips, lifting it up and letting it fall, over and over, until it looks like fine breadcrumbs. It's a calm, slow, repetitive job, and there's no hurrying it. Your hands grow warm. The kitchen is quiet except for the fire.

Then the sugar, stirred in. Then the spice, a little at a time, so that a warm, sweet scent rises from the bowl. Then the currants, dropped in by the handful, and turned through.

Then the egg, beaten, and a splash of milk, and you bring it all together with your hands into a soft dough, not too sticky, not too dry. You turn it out onto the floured table, and press it flat, and roll it, slowly, until it's about as thick as your little finger.

Then you cut the rounds. In a farmhouse kitchen, you might use the rim of a cup. One by one, you lift them onto the baking tray.

And now comes the part that made them soul cakes. With the back of a knife, or the edge of a spoon, you press a cross into the top of each one. Lightly. Just enough to mark it. In many places, that cross was part of the tradition, and it reminded everyone who ate the cakes that they were not just a treat, but a small prayer.

Then into the oven they go, or onto the hot bakestone by the fire. And you wait. The kitchen fills with the smell of butter and spice. You clear the table, and wipe the board, and wash the bowl, and the fire settles, and the window darkens.

When they come out, they're pale gold, with darker edges, and the cross shows clearly on each one. You set them on a cloth to cool. And you leave them there, under a clean cloth, ready for the morning, when the children will come to the door, singing.

1:41:47Bread for the Souls · 769 words

The giving of bread for the dead at this time of year was never only English. Across Europe, from Portugal to Poland, people baked something special at the start of November, and shared it, and thought of those they had lost. Let's take a short, slow journey through a few of those places.

We'll begin in the far west, in Portugal.

On 1 November, All Saints' Day, Portuguese children go from door to door with little cloth bags, sometimes sewn from patchwork scraps, sometimes with tassels. At each door, they recite a few lines of verse and ask for pão por Deus. Bread, for God's sake. And they're given bread, or small cakes, or sweet buns, or pomegranates, or dried fruit, walnuts, almonds and chestnuts. In parts of central Portugal, the day is called the day of the little cakes, and the children call out, bolinhos, bolinhos, at the doors.

It's an old custom. Records from the 1400s already give 1 November the name, the day of bread for God. The bread was shared with the poor, and it was bread given for the dead.

There's also a story, told in Lisbon, that links the custom to the great earthquake that struck the city on the morning of All Saints' Day, in 1755. After the earthquake, it's said, people who had lost everything went to the towns that had been spared, asking for bread for God's sake. That's a story people tell, rather than a recorded origin. The custom is much older than the earthquake. But the story shows how the day and the bread had become tied together in people's minds.

Now let's travel east, over the mountains and across France, to Austria and Bavaria, where the Alps rise behind the villages.

Here, at All Saints, the bakeries fill their windows with braided loaves. Long plaits of sweet yeast dough, made with flour and eggs and butter and raisins, a little milk, and a little salt, brushed with egg until they shine, and sprinkled with coarse sugar or poppy seeds. The loaf is called the Allerheiligenstriezel. The All Saints' braid.

It has other names too, from one valley to the next. One of them is Seelenwecken, which means something like soul rolls. Another is Seelenbrot, soul bread. The old link to the souls is right there, in the name.

In Austria, in Bavaria, and in parts of Hungary, it's the custom for godparents to give one of these braided loaves to their godchildren at All Saints. Imagine a child, on a cold bright November morning, walking with her parents to her godmother's house, and being handed a golden loaf, still faintly warm, wrapped in paper.

Further south, in Sicily, there's a custom that sounds a little magical. On the night between the first and 2 November, the dead are said to visit their families. And they bring presents for the children. Small toys, and sweets, are hidden around the house, and in the morning, the children search for them, and find them, and know that their grandparents and great grandparents, though they're gone, have remembered them.

There are special sweets in Sicily for this day too. Little figures made of hardened sugar, painted in bright colours and decorated with coloured paper and ribbons, which are called pupi di zucchero, sugar dolls. And there are hard, crunchy biscuits called ossi di morto. In English, that means bones of the dead, which sounds rather grim. But in Sicily, the idea is a warm one. People say that when you eat these biscuits, your dead go on living inside you. That remembering can be sweet.

And finally, let's travel north, to Poland. Here, the first two days of November are among the most important of the whole year. All Saints' Day, and then Zaduszki, the day of prayer for the souls. Families travel across the country to be together, the way they do at Christmas or Easter. And they go, together, to the graves of the people they have lost.

The roots of this go very deep. Long before Christianity reached these lands, Slavic and Baltic peoples kept an autumn festival for their ancestors, called Dziady, the forefathers. Food was left out for the spirits of the dead. Over the centuries, Dziady was gradually folded into the Christian days of All Saints and All Souls, and became, in a way, an early ancestor of Zaduszki.

Different countries. Different breads. Different songs. But the same simple idea, again and again. At the turning of the year, as the nights grow long, you bake something good, and you share it, and you remember.

1:47:45Lights for the Souls · 954 words

On the evening of 1 November, if you walk into a cemetery in Poland, you'll see something you'll never forget.

The cemetery glows. On every grave, there are candles. Not one or two, but dozens, in little glass jars, red and amber and clear and white, flickering in the dusk. Some graves are covered in them. Paths that would be dark on any other night are lit by thousands of tiny flames. People walk slowly between the rows, talking quietly, stopping to tidy a grave, to add a candle, to light one that's gone out. Children carry candles carefully in both hands. Old people stand for a long time, saying nothing.

From a distance, as night falls, the whole cemetery looks like a field of soft gold light, laid out under the trees.

That's what it looks like today. But the idea behind it is very old. Light for the souls. A small flame, kept burning, as a sign that someone is remembered. As a kind of prayer without words.

In medieval England, there were lights for the dead too. In our village church, around 1500, families paid for candles to burn before the images of the saints, in memory of the people they'd lost. Parishes kept lights burning for the souls, paid for by gifts and bequests. On All Souls' Day, as we saw, candles stood around the hearse in the nave, and some families set candles on the graves in the churchyard. And in Wales, families gave candles to the church, and watched the flames.

When the Reformation came, many of these lights were put out, along with the bells. But the idea of light in the darkness at this time of year didn't disappear. It turned up in turnip lanterns carried by children. It turned up in the hill fires of Lancashire on Teanlay night. And it turns up today, in candles on the graves, in many countries, from Poland to Portugal, and in candles lit quietly in windows by people who have lost someone.

Sometimes, at this time of year, it can help to light a candle of your own. Not for any ceremony. Just to sit with for a while, in a quiet room, at the end of the day, and watch the flame. The way it leans when a door opens somewhere in the house, and then straightens. The way it sends up a thin thread of smoke when it flickers. The small circle of warm light it makes on the table, and the soft darkness beyond.

People have been doing something like that, at the beginning of November, for a very long time. In medieval churches, in Welsh parishes, on Polish graves, and in ordinary houses all over the world. A little light against the long nights. A way of saying, you're not forgotten.

Let's go back, for the last time, to our village, on the night of All Hallows, around the year 1500. It's very late now. Midnight has come and gone.

In the church tower, the bells are still ringing, slowly, in their steady rhythm. The ringers have changed over again. Wat is asleep on the bench in the corner of the ringing chamber, curled up on a folded sack, his head on his arm. Old Roger has put his own coat over him.

Down in the nave, the candles are burning low. Hugh the clerk is sitting near the font, his chin on his chest, dozing, then waking with a start, then dozing again. A single lamp burns before the altar, as it always does, day and night.

In the churchyard, the grass is wet with dew. Somebody has left a candle in a little horn lantern beside a grave near the east wall, and it's still glowing, a tiny point of light in all that dark.

In the cottage by the lane, Agnes has banked the fire. The basket by the door is empty, the cloth folded. She lies in her bed and listens to the bells, the way she has listened to them every year of her life. When she was a little girl, she lay in this same cottage, perhaps in this same bed, and listened to them then. She thinks about her husband. She thinks about her mother, and her father. She thinks about her little one, who lived only a single year.

And she thinks, as so many people thought on that night, in so many villages, that they're not entirely gone. That somewhere, in some quiet, waiting place, they can hear the bells too.

And she sleeps.

Outside, the night goes on. The stars turn slowly over the church tower. The mist thickens in the hollows by the stream. A fox trots along the edge of the churchyard wall, stops, listens to the bells for a moment, and goes on its way. In the cottages along the lane, the fires sink to red embers, and then to grey ash, and the people inside sleep, wrapped in their blankets, while the bells ring over them.

Toward dawn, the ringers grow slower. The pauses between the rounds grow longer. Hugh, waking properly at last, climbs the stair with a jug of fresh ale and the last of the bread, and finds old Roger and Tom ringing on alone, steady and patient, with John asleep against the wall and Wat still curled on his sack.

And then, as the first grey light shows in the slatted windows of the bell chamber, Roger nods to Tom, and they let the bells swing lower, and lower, until they hang still. The last notes hum away into the morning. The night of All Hallows is over. And the feast of All Saints has begun.

1:54:40Goodnight · 254 words

Tonight, we've been a long way. We've stood in Agnes's warm kitchen as she marked each soul cake with a cross, climbed the narrow stair with the ringers, and walked with the children singing for soul cakes from door to door. We've been to Wittenberg on the eve of All Saints, and heard England's bells fall silent. And we've followed the old customs on, to the bread and sugar dolls of Portugal and Sicily, and the candles in the cemeteries of Poland. All of it, at heart, about one simple thing. Remembering.

Now, it's time to rest. Let the bells ring on, slow and soft, somewhere far away. Let the candles burn low, and the fire settle in the hearth. Think of Agnes, asleep in her cottage, with the empty basket by the door. Think of the last candle in the churchyard, burning low in its little horn lantern, and of all the people, five hundred years ago, lying in the dark and listening to the same slow sound, and feeling, for one night, that nobody was quite alone.

You don't need to do anything now. Nothing to remember. Nothing to finish. You can let the day go, the way the light goes from the fields at dusk. Slowly, and all at once. The ringers are going home now, down the lane, under the stars. Wat is asleep in his grandmother's cottage, warm under the blankets. And in the tower, one bell rings, very softly, one last time.

Goodnight. Until next time, sleep well.
